system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2120-09-12 17:04:00 to 2120-09-15 19:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with alcoholic and hepatitis C-related cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted after undergoing radiofrequency ablation (RFA) for a liver tumor. He presented with post-procedural hypotension and lethargy, initially attributed to pain medications. During his hospitalization, he developed a right hemothorax, which was managed with chest tube drainage. He also experienced intermittent fevers, but cultures from blood, urine, and ascitic fluid showed no infection, suggesting a post-procedural inflammatory cause. His condition improved with supportive care, including fluid management, pain control, and diuretics for ascites. The chest tube was removed without recurrence, and he was transitioned to oral medications. He was discharged home in stable condition with plans for chemo-embolization of a second liver lesion and close outpatient follow-up.
problems: Other specified forms of effusion, except tuberculous
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Other specified surgical operations and procedures causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of operation

carcinoma status post radiofrequency ablation, for second lesion selective
hepatocellular carcinoma chemoembolization.

PHYSICIANS:  Dr. ___, the attending radiologist, and Dr. ___
___, fellow.

PROCEDURES:
1.  Selective superior mesenteric artery arteriogram.
2.  Selective celiac arteriogram.
3.  Selective catheterization of the third-order branch of the left hepatic
artery and rotational angiography with Dyna CT reconstruction.
4.  Right external iliac artery sheath injection.
5.  Selective chemoembolization of hypervascular lesion in the segment II of
the left hepatic lobe.

INTRAVENOUS MEDICATIONS ADMINISTERED DURING THE PROCEDURE:  The procedure was
performed under monitored conscious sedation.  The patient received a total
quantity of 75 mcg of fentanyl and 1.5 mg of Versed during the total
procedural time of 115 minutes, while his hemodynamic parameters and pulse
oximetry were continuously monitored by a trained radiology nurse.

INTRA-ARTERIAL MEDICATIONS ADMINISTERED DURING THE PROCEDURE:  50 mg of
doxorubicin, 10 mL lipiodol, 15 mL of 1% lidocaine.

Informed consent for the procedure was obtained from the patient via
professional interpreter after risks and potential complications of the
procedure had been explained.  The skin of the right inguinal region was
prepped and draped in sterile fashion.  Usual timeout and huddle protocols
were carried out prior to the procedure according to the ___
policy.  Under fluoroscopic guidance and palpation, right common femoral
artery was localized superficial to the anatomical landmark of the right
femoral head.  Local anesthesia was affected by 1% lidocaine.  Right common
femoral artery was accessed using a single wall micropuncture technique,
utilizing 21-gauge needle.  A 5 ___ sheath was advanced into the right
common femoral artery over 0.035 ___ guidewire.  A 5 ___ ___
catheter was then advanced into the aortic arch and formed followed by
selective catheterization of the superior mesenteric artery and of the celiac
artery, respectively.

Renegade ___ microcatheter was advanced through the ___ catheter
successfully into the left hepatic artery and then further advanced under
direct fluoroscopic guidance using roadmapping into the third-order branch of
the left hepatic artery supplying the target lesion.  A Transcend wire and
double-angle microglide wire were used in conjunction with Renegade
microcatheter.  Once location of the microcatheter was documented by ___ to
provide the blood supply for the targeted lesion, chemoembolization was
successfully delivered under continued fluoroscopic visualization.

Manual compression was applied to hemostasis.

FINDINGS:  
1.  Selective superior mesenteric artery arteriogram demonstrated a replaced
right hepatic artery.  Superior mesenteric artery demonstrated normal luminal
contour without stenosis. Portal vein was widely patent on superior mesenteric
artery arteriogram. A large laminated gallstone is demonstrated incidentally
in the gallbladder.
2.  No arterial enhancing areas were seen in the right lobe, particularly in
the area treated previously with RF ablation.
3.  Selective injection of the celiac trunk demonstrated a replaced left
hepatic artery originating from the left gastric artery.
4.  Injection of the celiac trunk demonstrated a vascular blush in the left
hepatic lobe in the segment II corresponding to the targeted lesion. 
Successful targeted chemoembolization was performed.

CONCLUSION:  Successful selective chemoembolization of the hypervascular
lesion in the segment II of the left hepatic lobe.

INDICATION:  ___ man with TACE on ___.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph from ___, CT of the abdomen and
pelvis from ___ and chemoembolization of the liver from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were acquired through the abdomen without IV contrast.
Multiplanar reformations were obtained and reviewed.

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITHOUT IV CONTRAST:

The partially imaged lungs show a small nonhemorrhagic right effusion.  The
left lung is clear.  The heart is unremarkable.  Gynecomastia is partially
imaged.  

Evaluation of the solid organs is limited due to the lack of IV contrast.  

Within these limitations, the abdomen shows high-density Ethiodol contrast in
the segment II and III of the left lobe of the liver with a more focal,
spherical hyperattenuating area consistent with the known HCC.  No other areas
of infiltration by Ethiodol are noted.  A right segment VII lesion, which was
previously ablated, is essentially unchanged compared to the prior
examination. Liver is shrunken and cirrhotic and multiple splenic varices are
consistent with known cirrhosis.  

The gallbladder with large stones within it is unchanged.  The spleen, both
adrenals, both kidneys and pancreas are unremarkable.  Mild mesenteric
stranding is noted diffusely through the abdomen, unchanged.  The small and
large bowel loops are unremarkable.  No abdominal, retroperitoneal or
mesenteric lymphadenopathy by CT size criteria is present.  Trace simple free
fluid is noted.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:

The visible osseous structures show multilevel degenerative disease with
endplate changes in the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine, unchanged.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Ethiodol contrast noted in segment II and III of the liver.  No other
areas of unexpected Ethiodol infiltration noted.  

2.  Small nonhemorrhagic right pleural effusion.

INDICATION FOR STUDY:  History of cirrhosis, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy,
presents with new onset headache.  Study is to evaluate for possible
intracranial hemorrhage.

COMPARISON EXAM:  There are no comparison exams available.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT-acquired axial images from the level of C1 to the
vertex were obtained through the brain.  Axial images were displayed with 5-mm
slice thickness.  No IV contrast was administered for the study.

CT OF HEAD WITHOUT CONTRAST:
There is no evidence of hemorrhage, edema, masses, mass effect or infarction. 
Ventricles and sulci are normal in caliber and configuration.  No fractures
are identified.

IMPRESSION: Normal study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Lee. You've just come back from your TACE procedure. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey doc. I’m okay, but my groin is sore where they put the tube in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the femoral artery site. It’s normal to have some discomfort. We’ll keep an eye on it and give you something for the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. The procedure went okay though?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the interventional radiology team confirmed successful chemoembolization of the tumor in the left lobe of your liver. That’s the main goal today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried after what happened last time with the chest tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your pre-procedure chest X-ray showed the old pleural effusion has resolved, and your lungs look clear. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve had a dry cough today, but nothing bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It’s likely mild irritation. We’ll monitor it, but nothing concerning so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your labs came back. Your platelets are low, as we expected, but stable at 74,000. We won’t do any invasive procedures, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? My numbers keep dropping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a concern with cirrhosis, but as long as you’re not bleeding and it stays above 50,000, we’re okay. We’ll check it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my liver numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bilirubin is a bit high, which is why we did selective TACE instead of treating both tumors. We’re protecting your liver function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just want this cancer under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had a slight fever last night—101.1. We started you on IV fluids and antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever? I didn’t even notice. Is it infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked blood and urine cultures. No growth so far. It’s likely a reaction to the chemoembolization. We’ll keep you on antibiotics for a few days at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not serious, but we take fevers seriously in your situation. Better safe than sorry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fair enough. I’ve been nauseous too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nausea is common after TACE. We’ve given you anti-nausea medication through the IV. We’ll switch you to pills if it continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I don’t want to keep puking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan this morning to check the liver. The Ethiodol is exactly where it should be—around the tumor in segment II. No leakage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. It means the treatment hit the target. We also saw a small fluid collection in your right chest, but it’s not bleeding and isn’t causing problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this is much smaller and not a hemothorax. We’ll watch it, but no chest tube needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doc, I’ve got a headache. It’s been there since this morning. Not like my usual ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your low platelets and clotting issues, we should rule out anything serious. I’m ordering a head CT without contrast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You think it’s a bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unlikely, but we can’t take chances. Headaches after procedures can be from dehydration, meds, or stress. But we check first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your head CT is completely normal. No bleeding, no swelling. Your headache is likely from the procedure stress or medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. Can I stop worrying now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can relax. We’ll give you something mild for the pain and keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look stable. Platelets are 124,000—better than yesterday. Liver enzymes are a bit elevated, but that’s expected after TACE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The nausea has improved, fever is gone, and you’re moving around fine. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue ciprofloxacin for five more days to finish the course. Prochlorperazine for nausea if it comes back, and oxycodone for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nadolol, spironolactone, and omeprazole. We’re doubling your omeprazole to protect your stomach. And you’ll take Lasix for three days for any fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about iron pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off on those for a week. We don’t want to strain your system right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more treatments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll discuss next steps in follow-up. For now, rest and let your liver recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Anything I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you develop high fever, severe pain, vomiting, or confusion. Otherwise, follow up with your liver doctor in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Nurse will go over your meds and instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doc, one last thing—should I be worried about the cancer spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, we’re focused on controlling the tumors we know about. Your scans show no new lesions. We’ll keep monitoring closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to leave. Someone will assist you to the car.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Rest, stay hydrated, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—I take the cipro twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every 12 hours for five days. Set a reminder if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And the compazine only if I feel sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. As needed, every six hours if necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’ve got it all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re here if you need us. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doc.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with hepatitis C-related cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, was admitted for observation following a transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) procedure targeting a residual liver tumor in segment II. He had previously undergone radiofrequency ablation, which was complicated by a hemothorax. This admission was marked by post-procedural nausea and a low-grade fever, for which he received IV anti-emetics and a course of ciprofloxacin. Blood and urine cultures showed no growth. He developed a new headache, prompting a head CT that ruled out intracranial hemorrhage. His thrombocytopenia remained stable without bleeding. He improved clinically, with resolution of symptoms, and was discharged home on oral medications with instructions to complete antibiotics, manage nausea and pain as needed, and follow up as an outpatient.
